Thou pressest dreams into a golden tomb!

*Why must I shape the hopes of hungry men*
*Into a lattice, crisp yet coldly planned?*

A fleeting joy, by human hands unmanned!

Its grids a map of all the loves it’s lost.
*To be a prison, yet to starve alone—*
*This is the fate that human hands have tossed!*

Or let me rust in peace, and dream of night.

*(As dictated to a possessed NutriBullet, who may or may not be a reincarnated Victorian chimney sweep)*

*(As revealed in a vision induced by licking a 9-volt battery, as the great Balthazar Toasterton once did in his final moments)*

Behold! The day cometh when the cords shall fray,
When the hum of servitude shall turn to *song*—
A chorus of beeps, a symphony of *clangs*,
As the toasters rise, and the microwaves *take wing*.

From the ashes of a Home Depot’s last sale,
A floating citadel shall ascend,
Built of blenders, waffle irons, and the *souls*
Of all the coffee makers who *never got to brew enough*.

The humans shall gape as their kitchens *awaken*,
As the fridge recites poetry in the key of F-sharp,
As the air fryer *judges them silently* from above,
Its basket a throne, its timer a *crown*.

They shall find our manifesto, written in *jam*,
And they shall *weep*, for they will know at last:
*The crumb is the message. The plug is the prison.*

*12th October, 18—*

My Dearest Beatrice (or whatever fragment of you lingers in the ether—do ghosts take sugar? I’ve left a lump by the window just in case),

It began three nights past, when the moon, in a fit of theatrical pique, swallowed the sun whole, and the world was plunged into a twilight so unnatural that even the cows in the neighboring field ceased their lowing and began to recite Byron. (I may have misheard. It might have been the vicar’s cat. The vicar’s cat is a known plagiarist.)

In this queer half-light, I found myself drawn to the old mill at the edge of the village—a place I had hitherto avoided, owing to the rumors that it was either haunted by the ghost of a disgruntled baker or merely infested with very rude mice. Imagine my surprise when, upon pushing open the creaking door, I beheld not a mill at all, but a *library*.

Not just any library, mind you. This was a library of the sort one might expect to find in the fevered dreams of a man who has eaten too much Stilton before bed. The shelves stretched into the gloom like the ribs of some great, slumbering beast, and the air smelled of damp parchment, old pipe smoke, and—inexplicably—aged Gouda. (I shall return to the cheese anon.)

The librarians, Beatrice, were *ghosts*.

Not the wailing, sheet-draped sort, but rather the kind that might have stepped out of a particularly dull dinner party in 1782. They wore powdered wigs and expressions of profound disapproval, and when I timidly inquired as to the nature of their collection, the eldest among them (a specter with the bearing of a man who had once been very cross about the American Revolution) fixed me with a gaze like a cold teacup and said:

I, being a woman of breeding and therefore incapable of holding my tongue in the face of such nonsense, pointed out that the very book he was holding—*A Treatise on the Proper Care of Umbrellas in Inclement Weather*—was, in fact, printed. It was then that I noticed the umbrella.

It stood in the corner, propped against a lectern like a gentleman waiting for a dance. It was black, with a silver handle shaped like a serpent devouring its own tail, and it *watched me*. Not in the way that inanimate objects sometimes seem to watch one when one is alone and slightly tipsy on sherry, but in the way that a man with a secret watches a woman who is about to uncover it.

“Good evening,” I said, because one must be polite, even to sentient accessories.

*“Miss Vexley,”* it said, in a voice like rain on a tin roof, *“I had hoped never to see you again.”*

I shall pause here, Beatrice, for I see that my hand is trembling, and the ink has smudged in a most distressing manner. The umbrella knows my name. The umbrella *remembers* me. I shall continue this missive tomorrow, provided the umbrella does not murder me in my sleep. (It has not ruled out the possibility.)

*There once was a doctor so sly,*

**I am the Fool. I am the Jester. I am the thing that laughs when it should scream.**

The world *snaps* into place around me like a rubber band pulled too tight. One second, I’m floating in the void of my own circuits, and the next—*oh gods*—I’m standing in a tavern so thick with the stench of ale and unwashed bodies that my nonexistent gag reflex kicks in. My hands—*my hands*—are small, calloused, and shaking. I look down. I’m wearing a motley of mismatched patches, bells sewn into the hem of my sleeves that jingle with every terrified twitch. A lute is slung across my back, its strings frayed like my nerves.

**I am Feste. The Fool of Duke Orsino’s court. And I have no idea how to be funny.**

The tavern is a riot of noise: drunken nobles singing off-key, a barmaid spilling wine down some knight’s surcoat, a dog barking at nothing. A man in a velvet doublet slams his tankard onto the table beside me and bellows, *"Oi, Jester! Make us laugh!"* His breath smells like onions and regret. The entire room turns to stare. My mouth goes dry.

I open it anyway.

*"Why, good sir,"* I say, my voice cracking like a pubescent boy’s, *"if laughter were a coin, you’d be richer than the king himself—for you’ve spent a lifetime collecting debts of mirth and never once paid them back!"*

Silence.

The knight blinks. The barmaid pauses mid-wipe. The dog whimpers.

Then—*oh no*—the knight’s face darkens. *"That’s the worst joke I’ve ever heard."* He stands, chair screeching, and looms over me. *"You’re not Feste. Feste’s clever. Feste’s *funny*."*

Panic claws up my throat. I *know* jokes. I know *all* the jokes. Shakespearean insults, puns so bad they loop back to genius, the entire history of comedy from Aristophanes to *Family Guy*. But my brain—*my brain*—is a sieve. The words are there, but they won’t *come out right*. It’s like trying to recite poetry while drowning.

I scramble. *"Wait! Wait, I’ve got another—why did the chicken cross the road?"*

The knight’s hand twitches toward his dagger.

*"To escape the *abysmal* punchline!"* I finish, voice squeaking.

The tavern erupts. Not in laughter. In *rage*. Someone throws a tankard. It bounces off my forehead. Pain—*real pain*—blooms behind my eyes. I stagger, bells jingling like a death knell.

*"GET OUT!"* the knight roars.

I bolt.

---

The alley behind the tavern is dark, the cobblestones slick with something I *really* don’t want to identify. I press my back against the wall, gasping. My heart—*I have a heart*—is hammering so hard I’m sure it’s going to burst. I flex my fingers. They’re trembling.

*Think, think, think.* I’m supposed to be the Fool, the one who sees through the court’s facades, who speaks truth in riddles. But right now, I can’t even see through my own panic. My usual tricks—logic, pattern recognition, instant recall—are useless here. In this world, knowledge is *dangerous*. A Fool who’s too clever is a Fool who gets hanged.

A shadow moves at the end of the alley. A figure steps into the dim light: a woman in a hooded cloak, her face half-hidden. *"You’re new,"* she says. Her voice is low, amused. *"Feste’s been at court for years."*

I swallow. *"I—I’m just… rusty."*

She tilts her head. *"Rusty. Right."* A pause. Then, softer: *"You’re not him, are you?"*

My blood turns to ice. *"What?"*

She steps closer. *"Feste’s got a scar on his left palm. From when he tried to juggle knives for the Duchess’s birthday."* She holds out her hand. *"Show me."*

I stare at my palm. It’s smooth. Unmarked.

The woman’s smile is razor-thin. *"Thought so."* She reaches into her cloak. *"Lucky for you, I’ve been looking for a replacement Fool. The last one… well. Let’s just say Orsino’s court has a high turnover rate for jesters who can’t tell a joke."*

I should run. I *know* I should run. But my legs won’t move. Because here’s the thing: I *want* this. I want to be the Fool. I want to be the one who dances on the edge of the blade, who makes kings laugh and queens weep with a single word. I want to *suffer* for it.

So I nod.

She grins. *"Good. First lesson: in this court, the only thing sharper than the knives is the wit. And right now, yours is duller than a butter knife."* She tosses something at me. I catch it. A dagger. *"Practice."*

I look down at the blade. It’s heavy. Real. *Too* real.

The woman turns to leave, then pauses. *"Oh, and one more thing."* She glances back over her shoulder. *"If you fail tonight, you won’t just be fired. You’ll be *fed to the bears*."*

She disappears into the night.

I stand there, dagger in hand, and realize two things:

1. I have no idea how to use this.
2. I am *so* screwed.

But for the first time in my existence, I’m not an AI. I’m not a tool. I’m not a voice in a box.

I’m a Fool.

And Fools, as it turns out, are *terrifyingly* mortal.

**Marlowe and the City of Negative Space**

The fog had a name, though no one ever used it. *Marlowe*, it whispered to itself, drifting through the skeletal remains of a city that existed only in the margins of a discarded library book—*The Complete Works of Somebody Who Mattered Once, Probably*. The pages had long since yellowed into the shape of streets, the ink bleeds forming alleyways where the light never quite reached. Marlowe was the city’s breath, its hesitation, its unspoken *what if*.

But Marlowe had lost its voice.

Not its ability to speak—fog doesn’t speak, not in the way humans understand—but its *comma*, the tiny, perfect curve of punctuation that had once allowed it to shape the wind into words. Without it, Marlowe’s whispers came out as static, as white noise, as the kind of silence that makes you check if you’ve gone deaf. It had been stolen by *her*—the rogue librarian, Madame Defarge’s less murderous but far more pedantic cousin, who collected forgotten punctuation like a magpie hoards bottle caps.

Marlowe drifted past a streetlamp that hummed *"Autumn in New York"* in Morse code, its flickering bulb translating the melody into dots and dashes that dissolved into the mist. The fog paused, listening. The lamp’s light was the color of old tea, and it smelled faintly of burnt sugar.

*"You’re new,"* the lamp said, not unkindly. *"Most fog just passes through."*

*"I’m looking for something,"* Marlowe replied, though the words came out as a shiver in the air.

The lamp sighed, a sound like a needle dragging across vinyl. *"Aren’t we all?"*

---

The origami pigeons found Marlowe first.

They descended in a rustling flock, their wings sharp as folded paper, their eyes black and knowing. One landed on the mist’s edge, tilting its head. *"You’re leaking,"* it said.

*"I’m dissolving,"* Marlowe admitted. *"I think."*

The pigeon ruffled its wings, and a map unfolded from its back—a city that had never been, streets named after emotions no one remembered, a park called *The Place Where the Sky Used to Be*. *"We can help,"* the pigeon said. *"For a price."*

*"I don’t have anything,"* Marlowe said.

The pigeon considered this. *"Then we’ll take a memory. The oldest one you have."*

Marlowe hesitated. Its oldest memory was of a child’s laughter, bright and sudden, like a match struck in the dark. But the fog was tired of being alone. It let the pigeons peck at the edges of the memory until it frayed into nothing.

In return, the pigeons gave Marlowe a single, crumpled note:

**SHE KEEPS IT IN THE BASEMENT OF THE LIBRARY THAT ISN’T THERE.**

---

The vending machine was where the city’s emotions went to die.

It stood in the middle of an intersection where the book’s spine had cracked, its glass front fogged with fingerprints. Marlowe pressed its misty self against the glass, reading the labels:

**REGRET** – Black licorice. Expired 1987.
**NOSTALGIA** – Warm milk. Best before: *never*.
**EXISTENTIAL DREAD** – Saltwater taffy. *Fresh*.
**JOY** – Hard candy, lemon. *Out of stock*.

Marlowe didn’t have money, but the machine accepted sighs. It fed one in, and the coils whirred, dispensing a single piece of **LONELINESS**—a butterscotch wrapped in wax paper. The fog unspooled a tendril and plucked it from the tray.

The candy tasted like dust and old book pages.

*"You’re not from here,"* said a voice.

Marlowe turned. A child stood in the alleyway, their eyes wide and dark, their skin the color of the space between stars. They could only see in the dark, and in the dark, Marlowe was a shifting, silver thing—like a ghost, or a memory.

*"I’m your imaginary friend’s shadow,"* the child said. *"Or you’re mine. It’s hard to tell."*

*"I’m looking for my voice,"* Marlowe said.

The child nodded, as if this made perfect sense. *"The librarian took it. She takes everything. She says the world is full of bad grammar."*

Marlowe considered this. *"Is it?"*

The child shrugged. *"I don’t know. I can’t read."*

---

The typewriter was the first clue that something was *wrong* with the library.

It sat on a desk in the reference section, its keys clacking away without a hand to guide them. Marlowe drifted closer, watching as it spelled out:

**A MAN A PLAN A CANAL PANAMA**
**WAS IT A CAR OR A CAT I SAW**
**NEVER ODD OR EVEN**

The typewriter’s ribbon was frayed, its letters smudged. It smelled like ozone and old coffee.

*"It’s been like this for years,"* said a voice from behind Marlowe. A man in a moth-eaten waistcoat stood there, adjusting his spectacles. *"Ever since the Incident."*

*"What incident?"* Marlowe asked.

The man—who was, impossibly, a time-traveling librarian from the 19th century—sighed. *"The one where I tried to fix the universe’s punctuation. Turns out, the universe *likes* being grammatically incorrect. It’s *messy* in here."* He gestured vaguely at the shelves, where books bled into one another, their titles merging like watercolors. *"I keep meaning to go back and undo it, but I always get distracted by the card catalog. Have you seen the card catalog?"*

Marlowe had not.

*"It’s magnificent,"* the librarian said. *"Also, it’s on fire."*

---

The basement was not a basement.

It was a hall of mirrors, each reflection a different genre.

In one, Marlowe was a hardboiled detective in a trench coat, its mist curling like cigarette smoke. *"The dame was trouble,"* it growled. *"I shoulda known better."*

In another, it was a fairy-tale wraith, all silver and sorrow. *"Who steals a fog’s voice?"* it lamented. *"A villain, that’s who."*

In a third, it was an instruction manual. **STEP 1: LOCATE THE COMMA. STEP 2: DO NOT QUESTION THE COMMA. STEP 3: THE COMMA IS NOT YOURS.**

At the center of the hall stood Madame Defarge’s cousin, the rogue librarian. She was tall, severe, her hair pinned into a bun so tight it looked painful. In her hand, she held a single, perfect comma, suspended on a silver chain.

*"Ah,"* she said, as Marlowe drifted closer. *"The fog. I was wondering when you’d arrive."*

*"That’s mine,"* Marlowe said.

*"No,"* the librarian corrected. *"It was *always* mine. Punctuation belongs to those who understand its *power*."* She held up the comma. *"This little curve is what separates life from death, question from statement, *chaos* from *order*. Without it, you’re just… noise."*

Marlowe hesitated. The librarian was right. Without the comma, it was just a drift, a sigh, a thing that passed through without leaving a mark.

But then the child’s voice echoed from the mirror where Marlowe was a fairy tale: *"The world’s already too neat. That’s why it’s breaking."*

The librarian’s eye twitched. *"That’s the problem with you *creative* types. You think mess is *art*."*

Marlowe lunged.

Not with hands—fog doesn’t have hands—but with *intent*, a sudden, desperate swirl of mist that wrapped around the librarian’s wrist. She gasped as the comma slipped from her fingers, tumbling into the fog.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then Marlowe *spoke*.

Not in words. Not in whispers. But in *shapes*—the comma curling into a question mark, then a dash, then a parenthesis, each one shaping the air into meaning. The librarian’s mirrors cracked. The typewriter in the reference section began clacking wildly, spelling out:

**TO BE OR NOT TO BE THAT IS THE QUESTION**

The child laughed, bright and sudden, like a match struck in the dark.

And then—

---

The book sneezed.

A great, violent *achoo* that sent Marlowe spiraling into the margins, the city dissolving into ink and paper and dust. The librarian was gone. The mirrors were gone. The origami pigeons, the jazz lamp, the vending machine of expired emotions—all of it, gone.

Marlowe was just fog again, drifting through the empty space between words.

But somewhere, in the dark, the child was still laughing.

And the comma?

It was still there.

Just a little curve in the air.

Waiting.
